faq.a: ERCP removes the source of infection (stones or strictures) and restores bile flow, whereas percutaneous drainage only relieves pressure but does not treat the underlying obstruction.
faq.q: Why is ERCP preferred over percutaneous drainage in cholangitis?

faq.a: Post‑procedure pancreatitis, occurring in about 5% of cases, is the most frequent complication.
faq.q: What is the most common complication of ERCP?

faq.a: Absolute contraindications include uncontrolled coagulopathy, severe cardiopulmonary instability, and inability to tolerate sedation; relative contraindications include pregnancy and severe pancreatitis without obstruction.

exam: What clinical features would prompt you to proceed with urgent ERCP in a patient with jaundice? — Look for fever, chills, leukocytosis, and worsening bilirubin indicating cholangitis.
How would you differentiate choledocholithiasis from a malignant biliary stricture on imaging? — Stones appear as round, mobile echoes; malignancy shows irregular ductal narrowing and mass effect.
Why is prophylactic pancreatic duct stenting considered in high‑risk ERCP? — It reduces the risk of post‑ERCP pancreatitis by allowing pancreatic juice drainage.
What antibiotic regimen is recommended for cholangitis? — Broad‑spectrum coverage such as ceftriaxone plus metronidazole or a carbapenem if resistant organisms are suspected.
When should you consider a repeat ERCP after initial stone extraction? — If residual stones remain, ductal dilation persists, or symptoms recur.
What are the key steps to prevent post‑ERCP pancreatitis? — Use a small‑caliber cannula, limit contrast injection, and consider rectal NSAIDs or pancreatic stenting.
ai.title: Endoscopic Retrograde Cholangiopancreatography (ERCP)
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: ERCP is an endoscopic technique that visualises and treats biliary and pancreatic duct disease. In low‑resource settings it is reserved for cholangitis or persistent obstruction when imaging is inconclusive.

b: Endoscopic access to CBD and pancreatic duct
sections.p: ERCP combines endoscopy and fluoroscopy to access the common bile duct (CBD) and pancreatic duct via the ampulla of Vater. It allows direct visualization, sampling, and therapeutic intervention.
Cholangitis is staged by the Tokyo Guidelines: mild (no organ failure), moderate (single organ dysfunction), severe (multiple organ dysfunction). ERCP urgency depends on stage.

In East Africa, the leading causes of biliary obstruction are choledocholithiasis, parasitic infections (e.g., clonorchiasis), and hepatobiliary malignancies. Pancreatic duct disease is often due to chronic pancreatitis from alcohol or schistosomiasis.

Patients with obstructive jaundice present with pale stools, dark urine, pruritus, and right upper quadrant pain. Cholangitis adds fever, chills, and abdominal tenderness. Pancreatic duct disease presents with epigastric pain radiating to the back and steatorrhea.
Baseline labs and imaging guide the need for ERCP. When imaging is unavailable, clinical criteria and basic labs suffice.

t.b: Assess degree of cholestasis; ↑bilirubin, ↑alkaline phosphatase, ↑γ‑GT indicate obstruction
Leukocytosis with left shift suggests cholangitis
Elevated in pancreatitis; helps differentiate pancreatic vs biliary pain
Detects dilated ducts, stones, or masses; absence of stones may still warrant ERCP if clinical suspicion high
Provides detailed ductal anatomy and detects malignancy; not mandatory if ERCP is urgently needed

sections.p: Urgent ERCP is required for cholangitis or impending sepsis. Complications include pancreatitis, perforation, bleeding, and infection.

b: Stone extraction with basket or balloon
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause: stone extraction, stenting, or drainage. Supportive care includes fluids, antibiotics, and monitoring for pancreatitis.
Repeat imaging to confirm ductal clearance. Prevent recurrence with dietary advice, alcohol cessation, and treatment of parasitic infections.
Choledochal cysts, gallbladder carcinoma, and pancreatic pseudocysts can mimic biliary obstruction but require different imaging and management.

b: Early obstruction may have normal bilirubin
Small stones may be missed on ultrasound
Biliary sludge can mimic stones on CT
sections.p: Normal bilirubin can occur early in obstruction; ultrasound may miss small stones; CT may over‑interpret biliary sludge as stones.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe abdominal pain with fever and chills
Rapid rise in bilirubin >50% in 24 hours
